rule: adjusted_score desc, total_score desc; dedupe by arXiv id / URL / id / title

papers.title: Stable and Granular Policy Optimization for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Muyu Zou, Haibo Xing, Hao Deng, Zhezheng Hao, Jinxin Hu, Jiawei Chen, Yun Chen, Yu Zhang, Xiaoyi Zeng
papers.summary: Generative recommenders decode sequential semantic IDs for items, and because core metrics are scored at the sequence level, reinforcement learning is a natural fit. Off-the-shelf group-based algorithms struggle here: token-level methods become much more unstable, while sequence-level methods weight every token equally and ignore their different roles. A group-based method built for this setting keeps a sequence-level ratio for stability while injecting token-wise advantages. It upweights high-confidence tokens on positive trajectories to reinforce successful retrieval, strictly penalizes them on negative ones to encourage exploration, and uses an adaptive scale to bound the variance of the reshaped advantages. On two public benchmarks and a billion-scale industrial dataset, it consistently beats six strong reinforcement-learning baselines. In an online test on a commercial platform, click-through rate rose 2.36% and advertising revenue rose 1.95%.

papers.title: Better Rankers, Worse Retrievers: The Hidden Cost of RL Post-Training in Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Yuheng Chen, Fan Zhang, Yixuan Xu, Chao Yang, Yang Xiang, Can Yang
papers.summary: Post-training generative recommenders with reinforcement learning after supervised fine-tuning is now standard, but gains are usually reported on the first ten results, while deployed models often hand hundreds of candidates to a downstream ranker. A systematic measurement shows that reinforcement learning improves accuracy at the very top, yet on all five datasets studied it lowers recall of the candidate list: the model becomes a better ranker and a worse retriever. The cause is that only one next item is logged per user, so the most plausible alternatives in the rollout are treated as wrong and given negative advantages, and items that similar users would choose next drop out of those lists. An out-of-rollout anchoring term that preserves the supervised model's ordering of items outside the rollout keeps the gain at the top and restores recall to the supervised level on all five datasets. On Office, hit@500 falls from 52.84% to 47.69%, which shows how large this hidden cost can be.

papers.title: Keep it Simple! A Multiple-Choice Task can Benefit Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Wei-Hsiang Huang, Jyun-Yu Jiang, Pu-Jen Cheng
papers.summary: Generative recommenders often predict the target item's SID directly and never explicitly learn negatives or relative ranking, which sits poorly with the idea behind BPR, where the rank of a positive against negatives matters. Adding a simple multiple-choice auxiliary task to the learning objective, and synthesizing its training data with task identifiers and candidate construction, supplies that comparison signal with only a small change. A theoretical analysis from information theory and compositional generalization also argues that the auxiliary task helps the model learn a more stable and composable representation. On four public datasets, NDCG@10 rises 4.9% to 79% relative to the conventional generative model TIGER, lowest on MovieLens and highest on Yelp. Gains first rise with more candidates, then saturate. The results are already competitive with mainstream generative recommenders, and they do not rely on heavy tuning. For generative recommenders, adding relative comparison can come before a more elaborate architecture.

papers.title: HyMiRec: A Hybrid Multi-interest Learning Framework for LLM-based Sequential Recommendation
papers.authors: Jingyi Zhou, Cheng Chen, Kai Zuo, Manjie Xu, Zhendong Fu
papers.summary: When large models are used for sequential recommendation, latency and feature-bandwidth limits often force the system to truncate behavior sequences to recent interactions, dropping long-range preferences; predicting a single embedding also struggles to cover a user's many interests. A hybrid multi-interest framework uses a lightweight recommender to extract coarse interests from long sequences and a large-model recommender to refine them, and a residual codebook based on cosine similarity compresses and reuses history embeddings to cut feature-fetch cost. A disentangled multi-interest module uses multiple queries to learn different facets of intent. On public benchmarks and industrial data it improves over existing large-model methods, with an average gain of 24.53% on PixelRec and 8.9% on MovieLens-1M. In an online test, pass-through rate on image-and-text traffic rose from 26.46% to 30.93%, showing that long sequences and multiple interests can fit an online budget.

papers.title: ReSID: Rethinking Long-Tail Retrieval in Generative Recommendation through Item Reachability
papers.authors: Muyu Zou, Shunye Tang, Yi Xu, Haibo Xing, Yandong Wang, Lingyu Mu, Jinxin Hu
papers.summary: Generative recommendation encodes each item as a string of Semantic ID tokens and generates them one position at a time with beam search, and cold long-tail items are hard to retrieve this way. The authors take apart the whole chain from encoding through decoding to matching and find that tail items are mostly lost early in decoding: on Amazon Industrial, 62.5% of tail targets have already fallen out of the beam after just two tokens. They also find that parallel SIDs, which split the vector into segments and quantize each separately, treat the tail better than sequential SIDs that quantize residuals layer by layer. The reason is that an error at one position does not spill into later ones, so a partly wrong sequence still keeps useful positions. ReSID therefore damps popularity bias and adds a user-semantic score inside beam search so tail prefixes survive, then allows a match even when some positions disagree. It now serves main traffic, raising ad revenue by 1.3% and the long-tail exposure share by 4.0%. ==Tail items are often pruned during decoding, and looser matching afterwards cannot bring them back==.

papers.title: More Than What Was Chosen: LLM-based Explainable Recommendation Beyond Noisy User Preferences
papers.authors: Chung Park, Hyeongjun Yun, Taesan Kim, Junui Hong, Dongjoon Hong, Mira Myong, Jihoon Oh, MinCheol Cho, Kijung Park, Min ...
papers.summary: Recommenders usually assume that observed choices faithfully reflect underlying interests, but real-world choices are often noisy and inconsistent, so even large-model recommenders with reasoning may miss genuine preferences and produce unconvincing rationales. One approach complements revealed preference with a coherent-preference signal that favors items logically and causally consistent with interaction history, and jointly optimizes both in a unified ranking. The influence of each signal is adjusted depending on whether the two agree or conflict, so the model can learn from chosen items without being tied to a single noisy click. On Amazon review data, the method consistently outperforms about 20 strong baselines in both recommendation performance and rationale quality, and it achieved a 1.65 times relative improvement in click-through rate after deployment. For teams that want large models to recommend and explain, ==clicked items should not be treated as the whole of user interest.==

papers.title: TriGen: A Generative Paradigm for Trigger-Induced Recommendation
papers.authors: Muyu Zou, Haibo Xing, Shunye Tang, Liyan Tie, Lingyu Mu, Yandong Wang, Jinxin Hu
papers.summary: E-commerce has a common kind of recommendation: a user clicks an item in the main feed and lands at once in a feed built around that item. The recommendations must follow the intent of that click without throwing away the user's long-term taste. Generative recommendation by default just continues the user's history with more SIDs, so one click is easily diluted in a long history, while traditional methods rely on discriminative scoring and cannot steer token-by-token generation. Alibaba International's TriGen appends several copies of the clicked item to the end of the history so it mainly reshapes recent behavior. It then uses a gate to decide per request whether to follow the click or the history more, and keeps injecting the click signal at every decoding position. In online experiments in six Southeast Asian countries, revenue rose 3.27% and GMV 0.90%, and it is now fully deployed. ==In click-triggered feeds, the hard part is how much the click should override history, and that changes every time==.

papers.title: Hyperbolic RQ-VAE enhanced Generative Recommendation with Differential-Length Codebook Strategy
papers.authors: Aoran Zhang, Yu-Bin Yang, Yonghong Yu
papers.summary: When large models are joined with generative recommendation, most methods still run residual quantization in Euclidean space and only implicitly model hierarchy across codebook layers, which can distort a tree-like structure and leave codebook utilization low. A hyperbolic residual-quantization method embeds the discrete latent representations in hyperbolic space to model that hierarchy explicitly. Motivated by the exponential volume growth of hyperbolic space, it also uses a pyramidal, differential-length codebook, which aligns with the tree structure and compresses codebook size. After the geometry and the codebook hierarchy are aligned, collision rates are lower, codebook usage is more uniform, and training takes less time than existing methods. Across multiple benchmarks, the approach consistently reaches the strongest reported generative-recommendation results. For teams that assign semantic IDs to items, ==hierarchy is worth expressing directly in the geometry==, not only approximating it layer by layer with residuals.

papers.title: IntentGR: Enhancing Intent for End-to-End Personalized Generative Retrieval in Search
papers.authors: Gefan Ye, Yanjing Wu, Yinfu Feng, Zhiqiang Wang, Liang Li, Jun Xiao, Rong Xiao, Xiaoyi Zeng
papers.summary: Personalized generative retrieval in search needs to satisfy both the current query intent and longer-term preference. Existing end-to-end methods often treat the query as just another input feature, without using it to guide identifier learning or sequence generation, so the generated semantic IDs drift toward frequent token patterns rather than what the query is looking for. An intent-enhanced framework adds query-related evidence at four stages of the retrieval pipeline: it brings in query-level behavioral evidence as a new input, then applies semantic alignment, long-tail query enrichment, and query-conditioned attention at the optimization, training-distribution, and decoding stages. On the public AOL4PS benchmark and a large-scale industrial e-commerce dataset, it raises Recall@10 by 8.11% and 11.96% over the strongest baseline, with especially clear gains on long-tail queries. The implication is that ==end-to-end generative search should write query evidence into identifier learning and decoding==, rather than treating the query as a mere prefix.

papers.title: CARE: Contrastive-Anchored Residual Encoding with Listwise Reconstruction for Retrieval-Oriented Semantic IDs
papers.authors: Yuan Xu, Dawei Chen, Xiaoguang Lin, Xin Chen, Yulong Ou, Haijun Wu
papers.summary: Generative retrieval produces a document's SID, so where the tokenizer puts quantization error directly limits what can still be recalled. Common SID methods quantize residual codes on document embeddings alone and do not check whether a query can still find its relevant documents after quantization. CARE-SID first trains contrastive alignment in a retrieval-aligned space, then quantizes, while encoding still uses only the document's own embedding. In offline evaluation, reconstruction-view Recall@10 is 2.48 points higher than RQ-KMeans, and the tokenizer is used in the generative retrieval stage of an industrial video search system, where new videos can be encoded incrementally with the same weights. Listwise distillation can raise the score further, but the present gain mainly follows the reconstruction path; end-to-end benefit for a generator that consumes only integer SIDs still needs confirmation. The choice of embedding moves SID recall far more than the choice of quantizer, and contrastive alignment helps most when the embedding was not trained on search data.

papers.title: TokenFormer V2: Breaking the Resolution-Complexity Dilemma in Unified Recommendation
papers.authors: Kaihui Wu, Guoming Li, Liang Guo, Yifeng Zhou, Yuehong Hu, Junwei Pan, Zhixiang Feng, Chengguo Yin, Wenqi Fan, Haijie Gu...
papers.summary: Industrial recommenders need fine-grained long behavior histories, yet they must stay inside a strict serving budget: keeping every event is expensive, and compact summaries throw evidence away. This work decouples representation resolution from interaction density. It encodes behaviors in local groups, expands range through hierarchical merging and global synchronization, and still lets the final predictor read every encoded event directly. On the Tencent Advertising Algorithm Competition public benchmark, AUC rises 0.10 percentage points over MixFormer, the strongest unified backbone, while forward FLOPs are only 19.5% of that baseline. The lead remains on longer and more imbalanced histories. In a live traffic test on WeChat Channels ads, GMV rises a statistically significant 2.33% over the production model. ==Fine-grained history does not have to be compressed before it can fit the budget==. For teams choosing a unified ranking backbone, this is an organization already tested online.

papers.title: COTTI: Contrastive Training and Time-Aware Inference for Robust Industrial Recommendation under Promotional Drift
papers.authors: Maolei Huang, Jing Tian, Dexuan Duan, Fangfang Lin, Huawei Cao, Shuhan Song
papers.summary: Promotional events rewrite traffic mix, purchase behavior, and conversion probabilities across time horizons, so scoring with historical interest representations often fails when the event starts. A production recommender separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment: it aligns paired histories of the same user, down-weights promotional examples far from historical interest, and adjusts the output with a temporal event kernel while leaving the predictor frozen. In a ten-day online test covering one quarter of live traffic, conversion rate rose 3.14% and revenue per mille rose 2.68% relative to the serving model, with end-to-end p99 latency of 38.9 milliseconds. Cross-category analysis also shows a trade-off: better overall discrimination can come with lower paid-item recall in novel categories. ==Promotional recommenders must watch aggregate prediction and novel-category discovery together.==

papers.title: Lost in the Funnel: Selection-Induced Miscalibration in Ranking and Decision Systems
papers.authors: Aditya Somani, Rahul Ragesh, Vikas Joshi, Amit Singh
papers.summary: Multi-stage ranking often treats a score calibrated at the model boundary as a probability through filtering, reranking, business rules, and auctions, yet calibration is usually checked only where the score is produced. An industry diagnosis finds that decision-time expected calibration error rises four- to fivefold, and the breakdown comes from selection rather than model error: even a well-calibrated score can break after later filters. In a live two-region production test, selection-aware post-hoc recalibration at the decision boundary cut pre-auction calibration error by 60% and 71%. Impression-stage error fell by 63% and 80%. Auction efficiency improved, with no significant change in revenue. For multi-stage scoring systems the implication is direct: ==calibration has to be rechecked at the decision boundary==, not only at the model output.

papers.title: CLEAR: Legible and Steerable Recommendation via Grounded Natural-Language Interests
papers.authors: Qi Guo, Reza Mirghaderi, Iordanis Fostiropoulos, David Fan, Yuchen Liu, Shiliang Tang, Lukasz Korycki, Golnaz Ghasemiesf...
papers.summary: Recommenders often bury user taste in hidden vectors that people cannot inspect or change, so adding or suppressing an interest usually has no handle. CLEAR, deployed at Meta, adds an editable natural-language interest layer: each interest is grounded in the user's own history and serves as an address for retrieval, ranking, and exposure control. A newly declared interest can enter the candidate set through topical retrieval even before behavioral support exists. In direct user review, about 88.5% of displayed interests were rated accurate. For a newly declared interest, removing interest-conditioned candidate sourcing in the tested sequence cut same-day delivery by 13.7 percentage points. Components have run in production for more than a year across four surfaces on Instagram and Facebook. ==An interest has to be readable and able to change what gets ranked==. For products that want people to direct recommendations, this hooks a legible interest layer into the existing serving path.

papers.title: When Does a Recommendation Spark Curiosity? Theory, Measurement, and Field Evidence
papers.authors: Pan Li, Alexander Tuzhilin
papers.summary: Recommenders are often asked to break users out of filter bubbles, yet a user's curiosity has never had a definition a system can compute. Existing proxies such as unexpectedness and variety-seeking only look at how far an item sits from the user's taste. Picture two videos equally far from that taste: the user has watched many items similar to the first and none similar to the second. Distance scores them the same, but curiosity needs partial knowledge, so only the first makes the user aware of something missing. The authors turn the information-gap theory from psychology into five axioms and derive a curiosity score computed from consumption records alone, which matches self-reported curiosity in a survey. With this score added to the ranking objective next to relevance, an online experiment on a large Asian video platform raised click-through by 2.75 percentage points and watch time by 0.71 minutes per recommendation, and the method is now deployed. ==Curiosity depends on how much the user already knows, and distance alone cannot measure it==.

papers.title: Serving-Aligned Entire-Space Conversion Modeling via Click-Through Rate Knowledge Distillation
papers.authors: Pavel Dolin, Xun Zou, Jiatian Wu, Deguang Kong
papers.summary: Ranking often multiplies a click-through prediction by a conversion prediction to get the probability of a click followed by a purchase. Many conversion models are trained with ESMM, which carries its own auxiliary click-through tower trained together with the conversion tower, but only the conversion tower is deployed and multiplied by a separately trained production click-through model. The trouble is that the conversion tower was trained alongside the auxiliary tower's click rates, while in serving it is multiplied by the production model's click rates, so the product drifts when the two disagree. The Reddit authors leave the production click-through model alone and distill ESMM's auxiliary tower from the production click-through scores already stored in the logs, so the tower matches the production model during training. On Ali-CCP, the best setting raises PR-AUC of the product actually used in serving by 9.9%, and the conversion tower itself improves too. The gain survives when only 5% of negatives are kept. ==In joint multi-tower training, the auxiliary tower should learn the model it is actually paired with in serving==.

papers.title: Take a Step Back: A Dual-Granularity Raw Feature Empowered Intermediate Fusion Graph Convolutional Network for Multimodal Recommendation
papers.authors: Jinfeng Xu, Zheyu Chen, Shuo Yang, Jinze Li, Wenhao Yuan, Ziyue Peng, Puzhen Wu, Shujie Li, Jian Chen, Zheng Lin, Edith ...
papers.summary: Multimodal recommenders try to learn multi-level representations from sparse interactions, and often use contrastive learning to align modalities, which can squeeze out information that is unique to one modality. This work suggests taking a step back: large models generate coarse and fine raw features before training, as a complement to the original item features, rather than replacing the original text and images. An intermediate-fusion graph convolution network with dynamic cross-modality weight correction then captures cross-modality signals, instead of first forcing every modality into the same direction. On four standard Amazon datasets, Recall@20 rises 3.54% to 8.81% relative to MambaRec, the strongest baseline, and the gains remain under higher sparsity and item cold start. The model can also still benefit from additional alignment tasks. For graph-based multimodal recommenders, granularity need not be learned only from sparse interactions, and fusion need not rely on alignment alone.

papers.title: Cluster-Guided Decoding with Trust-Region Constraints for Personalized Recommendation
papers.authors: Gezheng Wen, Chao Shen, Raviteja Anantha, Tan Shen Cliff Chung, Layne C. Price
papers.summary: Most recommenders score each catalog item separately and never explicitly constrain which semantic region a recommendation should land in, while models that can offer that control are often too slow to run over a full catalog online. A cluster-guided generative method learns a hierarchy of semantic clusters and adds a cluster-level prior directly to the item scoring rule, rather than using clusters only to pre-select candidates. Because the prior is built from cluster centroids, it remains defined for cold-start users with no history. Across movie, game, and local-business benchmarks, the method beats classical, neural, and large-model baselines on every reported recall and ranking metric, lifting Recall@10 by 37% to 127% over the strongest baseline, with larger gains as the catalog gets sparser. It serves recommendations in milliseconds, making it a candidate for low-latency first-stage retrieval.

papers.title: PreDiff: Sequential Recommendation by Denoising Preference Distributions
papers.authors: Yaoqi Chen, Jianjin Zhang, Qi Chen, Weihao Han, Yujing Wang, Hao Sun
papers.summary: In sequential recommendation, a user's preference is usually concentrated on a small cluster of items that matter at that moment. Recent diffusion methods add noise to item embeddings and score candidates by similarity, so close items already have tiny score gaps and the most relevant candidates are the first to become indistinguishable under noise. Moving diffusion into distribution space, where each item gets independent noise, preserves rankings better, but it loses the semantic structure of embedding space and needs richer supervision than one-hot labels. A preference-diffusion method therefore projects preference scores back into embedding space while filtering low-relevance noise, and uses soft targets that encode inter-item similarity so the model can rank finely inside the preference cluster. On four benchmarks, it reports an 8% to 17% relative gain over existing methods.

papers.title: VAMIRec: Value-Aware Memory Intervention for Continual Recommendation
papers.authors: Xudong Zhao, Xiaolong Xu, Haolong Xiang, Xiaoyu Xia, Jiaqiang Zhang, Xuyun Zhang, Lianyong Qi, Wanchun Dou, Amin Behesht...
papers.summary: Continual recommendation has to adapt to new observations without indiscriminately discarding knowledge that is still useful. Existing methods mostly replay, distill, or regularize to limit forgetting, but noisy or obsolete inherited representations can clash with current preferences if they are preserved wholesale, and coarse global mechanisms are too slow when interests shift quickly. A value-aware memory intervention framework first splits inherited user memory into a slow anchor and a fast drift, then evaluates three candidate operations with conservative action values that account for uncertainty and intervention cost. Training-time action supervision is distilled into an inference-safe policy, and the chosen memory action is applied before all-item ranking. On three real-world datasets, the method consistently outperforms the strongest reported baselines. For incremental recommenders, ==whether to keep or revise memory should be chosen by value, not by blanket preservation.==

papers.title: IntentFlow: An Intent-Driven Real-Time Multimodal Search System with Image-Text Queries at Xiaohongshu
papers.authors: Dongjia Zhao, Yuchen Ma, Chunsheng Shi, Ziqiu Gui, Chao Yuan, Jianing Zhu, Zhaoxing Zhang, Yahui Liu, Daoxin Zhang, Yi W...
papers.summary: In user-generated-content communities, whether an image-text query matches a note depends on what the user wants to retrieve, not on visual or topical similarity alone. Reranking visual search results is not enough, because notes that fit the intent may never enter the candidate set. IntentFlow, deployed at Xiaohongshu, uses a hierarchical intent taxonomy so candidate retrieval and reranking share the same relevance criteria, and it builds training data and representations around those criteria. In a user-level online test, relative to the production control of visual search plus reranking, it raises Top-4 query click-through rate by 28.17%, query click-through rate by 18.96%, and average time spent on search results pages per user by 12.56%. ==Image-text search has to align on intent first, rather than fetching look-alike notes and trying to fix them later.== For community or multimodal search, intent belongs in retrieval, not only in the reranker.

papers.title: MIPR: A Benchmark for Reasoning-Intensive Multimodal Intent-to-Product Retrieval with Multi-Category Solutions
papers.authors: Qiang Li, Xuan Lu, Jian Ruan, Manxi Lin, Jiacheng Chen, Wen Shen, Zhihua Wei, Xiaoyu Shen, Dan Ou, Xiangheng Kong, Junju...
papers.summary: Real e-commerce queries often state an intent without naming a product, and the same intent may be fulfilled by items from several categories, yet most multimodal retrieval benchmarks assume a fairly well-defined target. A new intent-to-product benchmark provides 3,522 multimodal queries and a shared corpus of 30,731 products, with reasoning-intensive retrieval, multi-category solutions, and fine-grained relevance labels. The best embedding-based retriever reaches 49.23% nDCG@10 on the full query set, and reranking lifts that score to 60.11%, but large gaps to the candidate-pool oracle remain. When intent is clear yet not tied to a single category, retrieval is far from solved, and the benchmark is more useful as a diagnosis than as a single headline score.

papers.title: EchoSpec: Training Search Agents to Weigh Evidence Above Echoes
papers.authors: Shihao Yang, Can Zeng, Xinzhe Li
papers.summary: In real corpora, one claim is copied and paraphrased across many pages, while the primary source that settles a question often appears once. Search agents trained with reinforcement learning treat those echoes as if they were independent sources: eight paraphrased false-claim echoes overturn 58% to 73% of previously correct answers. EchoSpec first teaches the model to recover bridge entities past the echoes, then runs group reinforcement learning with an evidence-gated reward. On Qwen2.5-7B, it cuts deference to eight echoes by 30 to 44 points, and the gain transfers zero-shot to retrievers the model has not seen. Once the primary source is in context, the agent can overrule eight echoes as reliably as one. ==A search agent's failure is often not that it cannot answer, but that it stops searching before the primary source is in context.== For multi-hop question answering over open corpora, training should reward finding the original evidence, not only getting the final answer right.

papers.title: DetouR: Plugging Association Routes into Search Agents for Multi-hop Question Answering
papers.authors: Tingwei Chen, Yunxiao Shi, Zhendong Chu, Zhiying Deng, Min Xu, Qingsong Wen
papers.summary: Search agents for multi-hop questions usually follow semantic routes: they infer what is missing and phrase it as a query, so they only reach pages the model can name. The decisive page is often never named in the question, and is frequently just one hyperlink away from evidence already retrieved. Following those association routes reaches more gold pages under the same budget, but building a graph offline is costly, and relevance or fusion selection often drops linked evidence from the reader's limited context. DetouR is a plug-in that reuses the links that arrive with retrieved pages, and adds no extra search or language-model call: a light scorer reroutes near-repeat queries to linked pages, and personalized PageRank keeps evidence chains intact for the reader. Across four agents, it raises exact match by 4.0 points on 2Wiki and 1.4 points on HotpotQA, on average. ==The useful next hop is often not a query the model can name, but a link on a page already in hand.== For multi-hop search agents, association routes are a cheap complement to semantic search, without another retrieval or model call.

papers.title: From Relevance to Utility: Rubric Alignment in Yuanbao Search
papers.authors: Yu Lu, Lixin Zou, Yangqi Chen, Hui Xu, Qiaolin Xia, Hao Wang, Qianwen Ma, Reed Li, Shuang Zeng, Haijin Liang, Haibo Shi
papers.summary: Agentic search needs a search engine to assemble a document set that is useful for downstream reasoning, not merely to rank documents by per-document relevance. Prior work either improves isolated pipeline stages or applies reinforcement-learning selection on top of relevance-trained modules, leaving the full stack unaligned to utility for reasoning. A rubric-aligned framework derives, for each query, weighted positive and negative criteria from coarse to fine, then builds two training signals. A lightweight labeler distills rubric judgments into per-document utility labels that supervise a contrastive dual encoder and a multi-task ranker with four rubric-aligned heads, and a rubric-conditioned evaluator produces a set-level reward that drives a dual-branch reinforcement-learning selector. Deployed in Yuanbao Search, the pipeline improves end-to-end answer quality by 8.52% over the online production baseline.

papers.title: Fix Before Search: Benchmarking Agentic Visual Query Pre-processing in Multimodal Retrieval-augmented Generation
papers.authors: Shenglai Zeng, Jiankun Zhang, Kai Guo, Xinnan Dai, Hui Liu, Jiliang Tang, Yi Chang
papers.summary: In multimodal retrieval-augmented generation, text queries are often rewritten first, but visual queries are still treated as clean, fixed inputs. Real visual queries are frequently warped, degraded, or ambiguous, and retrieval can then fail badly. V-QPP-Bench casts visual query pre-processing as an agent decision: the model must diagnose the defect itself and call perceptual tools to repair the query. The evaluation covers 46,700 imperfect queries and a range of multimodal retrieval pipelines. Visual defects sharply lower retrieval recall and end-to-end performance; oracle pre-processing can recover near-perfect results, but off-the-shelf multimodal models still struggle to choose tools and predict their parameters, while supervised fine-tuning lets compact models match or surpass larger proprietary ones. ==A visual query should not be assumed clean; repairing it before search can matter more than swapping the retriever.== For image-text retrieval-augmented generation, query pre-processing deserves its own evaluation and training, rather than an assumption that the input has no noise.

papers.title: LMEG-Doc: Layout-Grounded Multi-View Evidence Graphs for Multimodal Long-Document Retrieval
papers.authors: Changcheng Fu, Xiao Liu, Qi Yu, Yage Wang, Derek Young, Giri Iyengar
papers.summary: When evidence in a long multimodal document is spread across pages and modalities, ranking each element only by its own similarity to the question can leave relevant figures and tables low in the list. LMEG-Doc first builds an evidence graph from layout and context, then uses a vision-language model to add relations across distant pages, and propagates multimodal retrieval scores along the graph so connected supporting evidence is recovered together. Retrieval improves on MMDocIR, DocScope, and FinRAGBench-V, and the method outperforms retrievers fine-tuned on MMDocIR without task-specific training. After the retrieved evidence is added to existing question-answering pipelines, answer accuracy with Qwen3.8-27B rises by 7.6% on DocScope and 15.8% on FinRAGBench-V. ==Long-document retrieval cannot score isolated elements alone; it also has to see layout and cross-page relations among them.== For question answering over filings or manuals, bringing connected evidence back together is often more useful than nudging single-element similarity a little higher.

papers.title: Deal With It: On Better Schedules for Listwise Reranking
papers.authors: Benjamin Clavié, Herumb Shandilya, Hanna Lichtenberg, Aamir Shakir, Makoto P. Kato
papers.summary: Listwise large-model rerankers cannot reliably rank hundreds of documents in one call, so they depend on schedules to orchestrate many calls. Parallel schedules split candidates into groups and advance a fixed quota from each; when a group holds more of the true top passages than its quota, some are cut, and expensive repair calls are required. How the candidates are split determines where that quota can bind. The analysis shows that dealing them round-robin by retriever rank is the best equal-quota split in expected cuts, and that contiguous chunks cut more as the retriever improves. The simplest schedule allowed by this analysis is on average within 0.1 nDCG@10 of the best schedules, and in existing schedules it reduces repair calls from 59% of queries to 14%, improving latency with no significant change in quality.

papers.title: LoCaR: Localized Canvas Retrieval With Frozen Vision-Language Model
papers.authors: Rahim Hossain, Dipanwita Saha, Ashirbad Mishra, Xinxin Shu, Svetlana Strunjas, Binbin Li
papers.summary: Whole-image embeddings often under-represent small objects and local attributes that localized queries need in order to tell relevant images apart. A training-free framework does localized text-to-image retrieval with frozen vision-language models: it builds independent region proposals so attention can sit on the object, then encodes each region separately with the frozen visual encoder. Optional paired-support adaptation is only a residual that uses matched text-region exemplars, without updating the underlying encoders. A Visual Genome-derived benchmark is introduced to evaluate localized retrieval for smaller and harder referents. Across several vision-language backbones, the main gain comes from improving the region representation itself; on CLIP, adding the optional adaptation raises region Recall@1 by 2.42 percentage points. Localized retrieval has to see the region clearly before it needs to fine-tune the whole model.

papers.title: Too much of a good thing: Why 20 candidates beat 200 when reranking search results
papers.authors: Scott Martens, Sofia Vasileva
papers.summary: Is it always better to give a reranker more candidates? Jina's team at Elastic tested its own listwise reranker on more than two dozen retrieval benchmarks, and the answer is no. With BM25 as the first stage, reranking the top 100 candidates works best, cutting about a fifth of the error on average, and adding more makes it worse. With semantic search as the first stage, the best point moves down to 20 candidates and the gain is much smaller, and sending 200 is on average worse than not reranking at all. The reason is that a listwise model reads the whole candidate list at once, so with too many candidates its attention is spread thin and noise accumulates. A model that scores candidates one by one does not have this problem, since an extra candidate never changes the order of the others. The worse the first stage, the more candidates reranking needs and the more room it has to fix things. ==Size the candidate pool by the quality of the first stage, because sending too many hurts==

papers.title: Efficient Wide-Beam Generative Retrieval with Model-Native Trie Decoding and Shared-Context Attention
papers.authors: Vedant Jhaveri, Arashpreet Singh Mor, Satyam Kumar, Alex Tsun, Qing Lan, Shaunak Mishra, Sriram Vasudevan
papers.summary: Generative retrieval maps requests to catalog entries as short semantic IDs, and trie-constrained beam search keeps those IDs valid, but wide beams create two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. A model-native output interface stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors, avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention reuses prompt key-value blocks across beams while keeping each beam's private decode tail. Implemented in SGLang and measured on a Qualification Retrieval Platform workload at beam width 200, the combined system raises closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57 times over a custom logit-processor baseline and by up to 2.63 times over BF16 FlashRec.

papers.title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
papers.authors: Tianhua Tao, Akshita Bhagia, Dirk Groeneveld, Pete Walsh, Tyler Romero, Yashas Samaga, Jacob Morrison, Iz Beltagy, Taira...
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts models add parameters, but the useful compute per token barely changes. If the training stack still moves and stores parameters as a dense model would, throughput falls as the expert pool grows. Olmo-core replaces fully sharded data parallelism with distributed data parallelism, and adds expert parallelism, pipeline parallelism, a distributed optimizer, and activation rematerialization. On B300 eight-GPU nodes, with up to 512 GPUs, a 1.2-trillion-parameter run that uses MXFP8 (a microscaling 8-bit float format) and per-layer rematerialization reaches 858 useful-model TFLOPS per GPU per second. The authors also find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides. ==Once experts multiply, the first bottleneck is moving parameters, not the math per step.== For teams training very large MoE models, parallelism, precision, and rematerialization have to be designed together, or useful compute is spent on traffic first.

papers.title: Efficient Distributed MLLM Training with Cornstarch
papers.authors: Insu Jang, Runyu Lu, Nikhil Bansal, Ang Chen, Mosharaf Chowdhury
papers.summary: Multimodal models stitch vision or speech encoders together with a language model, so both the architecture and the data are uneven. Dropping them into a language-model training stack often leaves pipeline stages and context-parallel ranks badly balanced. When an encoder is frozen, a pipeline cut that assumed every module was trainable falls out of balance; tokens of different types also attend over different ranges,. Cornstarch splits the pipeline with frozen modules in mind, and assigns tokens in context parallelism by attention work. On 24 A40 GPUs, end-to-end training throughput rises to 2.26 times that of existing systems on average; after the frozen state is built into the cut, an iteration can be up to 2.46 times faster. ==The bottleneck in multimodal training is often idle time between unlike modules and unlike data.== For teams training vision-language models, the parallel cut has to see frozen weights and attention masks, rather than reuse a text-only plan.

papers.title: KaleidoKV: Rearranging Evidence for Efficient KV Cache Reuse in Offline RAG Inference
papers.authors: Peiting Xie, Xingyu Tan, Xiangjun Zai, Chen Chen, Xiaoyang Wang, Wenjie Zhang
papers.summary: In offline batch question answering, related questions often retrieve overlapping evidence, but a prefix cache can be reused only when the token prefixes match exactly, so a different evidence order forces a recompute. Existing reordering methods lock groups too early, and the planner itself can spend the prefill it hoped to save. KaleidoKV plans evidence order across the whole batch, keeps a move only when it lowers planned prefill, and admits dependent requests only after their shared prefixes are ready. In all sixteen settings it records the highest throughput and the lowest mean time to first token, at about 1.24 to 1.75 times the throughput of the strongest baseline, including planning time. ==Evidence order is not a minor tweak; it decides whether the prefix cache can be shared at all.== For offline RAG batch inference, planning shared prefixes first and then controlling when requests enter the engine works better than tuning the cache one request at a time.

papers.title: NVFP4-MLA: Unified FP4 KV-Cache Storage and Attention Computation for Multi-Head Latent Attention
papers.authors: Chao Ni, Qi Zhang, Xiao Wang, Zongfei Jing, Mingyang Hao, Binghan Chen, Kefeng Duan, Yu-Jung Chen, Mengdi Wang, Tijmen B...
papers.summary: In long-context reasoning and agent workloads, multi-head latent attention already shrinks the KV cache with a low-rank latent, but the cache still grows with length and concurrency, and attention compute can saturate first. Pushing both storage and attention to FP4 is not a drop-in change: sensitive channels need a residual, and one latent cache must serve the two reduction directions of the attention matrix multiplies. On DeepSeek-R1, the method compresses the MLA KV cache by 3.20 times relative to BF16, and speeds up the attention kernel by up to 2.82 times over FP8. In disaggregated serving, per-GPU throughput rises by up to 2.30 times, while average accuracy across nine benchmarks still matches BF16. ==To get the benefit of 4-bit MLA, storage, the kernel, and the cache layout have to change together.== For teams raising concurrency on long sessions, making this shared latent cache truly 4-bit in compute pays off more than compressing storage alone.

papers.title: K2-Horizon: A Frontier Fleet of Open Source Language Models
papers.authors: K2 Team, Zhengzhong Liu, Haonan Li, Xuezhe Ma, Alexander Moreno, Subham Sekhar Sahoo, Rupesh Kumar Srivastava, Mikhail Y...
papers.summary: Open models that both match strong peers of the same size on reasoning and agent tasks, and also release their data, training process, and intermediate checkpoints, are still rare. K2-Horizon is a fully open fleet that runs from small dense models to a large mixture-of-experts model, and it also releases training logs and infrastructure code. Its 36B-A4B model uses mixture-of-value attention and, with about one-seventh the active parameters, nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data. Uno, a lossless diffusion adapter, speeds up the 7B model by about 2.2 times at batch size 1, without a separate draft model. ==Open weights are not enough; the data and the training process need to be visible as well.== For anyone who wants to reproduce or continue training an open model, a dense and sparse pair trained on the same data and recipe is more useful than a final leaderboard score alone.

papers.title: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.authors: Keiji Kimura, Yuma Ichikawa
papers.summary: In post-training quantization for large language models, GPTQ is the usual layer-wise solver, but it optimizes continuous group scales separately from discrete integer assignments, even though the two are coupled. JointQ, in group-wise quantization, recomputes a group's optimal scale in closed form whenever it changes one integer, and periodically re-solves all scales jointly. The search starts from candidates that include the GPTQ solution, so the unregularized layer-wise calibration error is never worse than GPTQ, and the weights stay in a format that can replace it directly. The gain in six-task average zero-shot accuracy grows from 0.0044 in a wide-group 4-bit setting to 0.1559 in 3-bit per-channel quantization, and the method beats vanilla GPTQ in fourteen of sixteen comparisons. ==At low bit-widths, scales and integers cannot be chosen by a greedy split.== For teams pushing models to 3-bit or to larger groups, fixing the solver itself may help more than preprocessing the weights alone.

papers.title: Making Preemption Productive in Long-Output LLM Serving
papers.authors: Ziji Shi, Xinyi Wan, Chaoyi Ruan, Guangxing Huang, Min Lin, Jialin Li
papers.summary: Reasoning models emit long outputs, and their KV caches can occupy a GPU for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request may repeatedly lose its state and then write few new tokens after it returns: cache thrashing. In the authors' replays, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in CPU memory, readmits requests by how long they have waited, and guarantees a stretch of steady decoding after they return. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds; P99 time per output token falls by 50.7% relative to recomputation in the same engine, and the replay finishes 10.7% sooner. ==Preemption cannot be avoided, but a preempted request should not lose the work it already did.== For serving long-output requests, keeping a snapshot and giving it an undisturbed decoding turn costs less than computing the same tokens again.

papers.title: MeltKV: Memory-Aligned KV Cache Compression via Variable-Bit Packed Vector Quantization for Long-Context LLMs
papers.authors: Jiyun Han, Seongjoon Cho, Seungkyu Choi
papers.summary: In long-context inference, the KV cache quickly fills memory and slows decoding. Existing vector quantization can push the cache below 4 bits, but when indices are not packed into standard word widths and codebooks grow large, the saved space and speed disappear. Some methods share a global codebook to decode faster, then lose accuracy at lower bit-widths; others keep accuracy, but decode even slower than an uncompressed cache. MeltKV assigns variable bit widths to grouped key channels, packs the indices into standard data types, and shares a codebook across attention heads, dropping the padding that alignment would otherwise add. At comparable perplexity, it uses 48.05% less memory than the MILLION method and cuts decoding latency by 52.91% relative to CQ, a vector quantization method, and it can compress the representation down to 1 bit. ==Going to fewer bits is not enough; the indices have to be packed to match memory alignment.== For teams raising concurrency on long contexts, memory and decode latency have to be read together, not just the compression ratio.

papers.title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
papers.authors: Xin Guo, Qiang Zhang, Xiang Zhou, Arushi Rai, Siyu Lin, Yifan Wu, Xiang Shen, Lei Huang, Qunshu Zhang, Xiangjun Fan, Liz...
papers.summary: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large models keep a natural-language profile for each user, then splice it into the prompt and recompute its key-value cache during prefill for every ranking call. Those calls are prefill-heavy, decode-short, and frequent, and prefix caching cannot help because the text before the profile changes from call to call, so repeated prefills dominate serving. One system stores profiles as reusable key-value caches instead of text. Lightweight LoRA writers trained by self-distillation emit that reusable cache while the profile is decoded, and the model can read it at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. A custom scheduler uploads the next batch's stored cache while the current batch runs, hiding host-to-GPU transfer behind compute. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, ranking quality shows no statistically significant difference from full prefill. Under saturated load, throughput of the downstream scoring path rises by 4.0 to 4.5 times.

papers.title: HandUMI: A Modular Hand-Worn Parallel-Jaw Interface for Robot-Free Bimanual Data Capture
papers.authors: Brik Meza, Leonardo Perez, Alvaro Mendoza-Li, Aniela Ubillus, Mitshell Ramos, Raul Bastidas, Mauricio Olivera, Bryan Bas...
papers.summary: Bimanual demonstrations usually occupy a robot during collection, and the motions are hard to move to a new body. A hand-worn parallel-jaw interface uses swappable fingertips to match the robot gripper, tracks the hands with headset controllers, and measures aperture with encoders. Bimanual demonstrations can therefore be captured without a robot and then retargeted by inverse kinematics to seven simulated bimanual arms, with median position error of at most 1.2 millimeters. On real PiPER arms folding a towel, an ACT policy trained on these robot-free demonstrations succeeds in 12 of 20 attempts, while the same policy trained on only an earlier slice of the data succeeds in none. The hardware and software are open source, and a pair with a Quest 3S stays inexpensive. For labs that need more bimanual data, ==demonstrations need not be bound to the target robot first.==

papers.title: What Makes a VLA Reactive? A Study of Execution Strategies for Dynamic Manipulation
papers.authors: Zhuoyue Li, Zhendong Han, Pankhuri Vanjani, Wenting Li, Rudolf Lioutikov
papers.summary: A VLA model predicts a short chunk of future actions at a time, and when objects move, that chunk goes stale before it finishes executing. The authors use a pretrained π0.5 on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. They systematically compare how far to predict, how many steps to execute each time, and synchronous or asynchronous inference. The best prediction length is about one second, asynchronous inference helps more when the execution horizon is short, and methods that keep successive trajectories continuous beat those that only reduce latency. The biggest surprise is the conveyor picking task. Fine-tuning the policy with reinforcement learning fixes targeted failures, but the same checkpoint with no training at all reaches 71% success just by setting the execution horizon to 5, as good as after training. ==How fast a robot reacts depends on how it executes as much as on the policy, so evaluate the two together==

papers.title: Scaling VLA Serving Under Robotic Execution Constraints
papers.authors: Yue Zhang, Zicong Ye, Lufang Chen, Dance Yang, Mingyang Li, Zhenwei Duan, Michael Zhao, Ziye Deng, Starrick Liu, Ruizhi ...
papers.summary: The authors' company already has hundreds of VLA-driven robots working in real environments, and robots must share GPUs to keep inference costs down. Robots keep executing old actions while waiting for new ones. So among requests of the same size, some robots are about to run out and need a reply now, while others can wait. Admitting one more request on the GPU also slows the requests already running, and once a robot's action queue empties it must stop and wait. XInfer breaks VLA computation into stages that proceed as soon as their dependencies are ready, and its scheduler uses each robot's current urgency to decide what to compute first and when a new request may join. On three VLA models with production-derived workloads, the number of robots one GPU can serve under real-time requirements is 1.26 to 3.75 times that of the compared systems. ==When serving a robot fleet, a request's urgency depends on how many actions the robot has left==

papers.title: Ego2Sim2Humanoid: Agentic Real-to-Sim for Learning Loco-Manipulation VLAs without Robot Demonstrations
papers.authors: Chen Liu, Nikolaus Correll
papers.summary: Egocentric glasses can record a person's demonstration without occupying a robot, but a person's stature and hand shape differ from the robot's, so copying the hand motion often misses the contact or fails to hold. This method reconstructs the scene from the glasses views and head trajectory, plans stances and grasps the robot can reach without penetrating the object, then completes whole-body motion in a physics simulator and renders training views from the robot camera. Fine-tuned only on this converted data, with no real-robot demonstrations of the target tasks, a whole-body VLA on a Unitree G1 lifts the bottle in nine of twenty trials (45%) and places the hat on the head in five of twenty (25%). ==Turn a human recording into a physically feasible robot trajectory first, then fine-tune==. For teams collecting loco-manipulation data for humanoids, recording can use only glasses and need not occupy the robot.

papers.title: ResWAM: Learning What Changes, Not What Stays, for World-Action Models
papers.authors: Chongyu Fan, Gaowen Liu, Ramana Rao Kompella, Jason Corso, Sijia Liu
papers.summary: Adding a future prediction to an action policy is meant to help the model anticipate how its actions will change the world. Over an action chunk, though, the image often barely moves, so a loss on the complete future is dominated by the static background. This work supervises only the residual from the current frame to a future frame in a frozen visual feature space, and that residual concentrates on the arm and the object being manipulated. The resulting residual world-action model has a few billion parameters and uses no pretraining on robot trajectories beyond the benchmark demonstrations. On real-robot Open, Put and Stack it reaches 80.0% average success, ten percentage points above the strongest baseline, at 92.7 milliseconds per action chunk. ==Learn what is changing in the image, rather than copying the unmoving background again==. For closed-loop use on hardware, compute can be spent on change, without carrying a heavy video generation model.

papers.title: Continually Evolving Skill Knowledge in Vision Language Action Model
papers.authors: Yuxuan Wu, Guangming Wang, Zhiheng Yang, Tianchen Deng, Maoqing Yao, Brian Sheil, Hesheng Wang
papers.summary: Vision-language-action models can accumulate knowledge in pretraining, but continual learning remains hard. Existing continual imitation methods often add parameters or modules, which does not scale well for large models. A knowledge-driven framework with no parameter growth jointly optimizes task representations and a self-evolving knowledge space, and routes experts using a knowledge posterior over relations and semantic embeddings for task specialization. It has two forms: one that is task-centric, and one that models reusable skills across tasks in a hierarchy. On LIBERO, the method stays strong against vision-language-action and continual-imitation baselines with only 1% replay, and dual-arm real-world experiments validate knowledge transfer across embodiments and scenes. The hierarchical variant is stronger at hierarchical manipulation, and visualizations show knowledge retention and task discovery. For robot models that must keep adding skills, ==a knowledge space can evolve without growing parameters to remember old tasks.==

papers.title: Hidden Variables Behind Real-Robot Data Quality: Lessons from Hundreds of Thousands of Hours
papers.authors: Maniformer Real-World Manipulation Team, Che Tsang Calvin, Xingyu Chen, Bowen Jiang, Naixiang Gao, Xiongfeng Cai, Enlin ...
papers.summary: As real-robot data collection scales, workspace limits, control-interface friction, and latency can write pauses, detours, and corrections into demonstrations that still count as successful. One study looks at these hidden variables across embodiment, teleoperation control, and data consistency, combining a kinematic study of 25 dual-arm robots, controlled teleoperation experiments, and real-robot evaluation of fine-tuned policies. Parallelizing body-part control cuts task completion time by 43% to 53%, and compliant control improves success while reducing peak contact forces on contact-rich tasks. Policies also keep about nine tenths of the extra path length in detour-contaminated demonstrations, so inefficiencies in the collection system are remembered by the model. Task success alone does not reveal demonstration quality. Better real-robot data starts with seeing what the workspace and the interface actually write into the trajectory.

papers.title: From Temperature-Limited to Battery-Limited Legged Locomotion
papers.authors: Raphaël Ségas, Balázs Opra, Léo Ghafari, Thomas Stewart
papers.summary: Sustained walking on legged robots often ends in thermal shutdown of a few joint motors, long before the battery is empty. One method trains thermally aware locomotion policies with reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrates this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. A lumped thermal network, fitted on runs of a single robot and calibrated to measured electrical power, predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean error below 1 degree Celsius across robots, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under load, a policy trained without thermal awareness hits thermal shutdown in about 19 minutes, while the thermally aware policy drains the battery after 174 minutes, still with headroom at the hottest motor. Sustained walking should reward lower predicted asymptotes of the hottest joints, not only whether the current gait can move.

papers.title: TMA: Sim-to-Real Forceful Humanoid Manipulation via Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation
papers.authors: Yiting Chen, Kelin Yu, Sarthak Kaingade, Bryan Trinh, Kaiyu Hang, Roberto Martin-martin, Nima Fazeli, X. Alice Wu
papers.summary: Humanoid whole-body work in hinged environments has mostly been about lining up geometry. Opening a round doorknob with force also means adapting in real contact, without losing whole-body balance. This method organizes policy learning around contacts the fingers can feel, and adapts motion online from tactile history. An upper-body policy is coordinated with a pretrained walking controller, trained entirely in simulation, and transferred zero-shot to a Unitree G1 with multi-fingered hands. In simulation, door-open success is 80.9% with the full tactile signal and 73.6% with contact presence alone. On four commercial knobs, ten trials each, with no real-world fine-tuning, it clearly outperforms adaptation from proprioception only. ==On a hand that cannot back-drive force through the joints, proprioception alone does not show how much force to apply==. For teams that want a humanoid to open a real door, force and contact history have to enter the adaptation loop.

papers.title: Learning Low-Latency Action Verification for Frozen Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Wen-Han Hsieh, Ken Jiankun Zheng, Chia-Chien Chen, David M. Chan, Trevor Darrell
papers.summary: The actions a VLA model samples are not always good, and sampling several and picking one is safer, but using a large model as the judge adds a long wait to every query. The authors' HDH trains its judge only on records from the frozen VLA's own deployments. The policy first runs a batch of tasks on its own and the final outcome after each action chunk is recorded. A small model then learns to predict, from the current view and the actions already executed, how likely a candidate chunk is to end in success. At deployment the VLA generates two candidates and the small model executes the higher-scoring one, with no expert labels and no predicted future frames. On four LIBERO-10 tasks, average success rises from 78.8% to 82.3% with only 5.4% more query latency, more accurate and faster than GPT-family judges, and the gain is larger on three real-robot tasks. ==A robot's own record of successes and failures is enough to teach a cheap action judge==
